🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.11% (intraday, 7-year +16bp). At trading day 15 (last close) it was -1.43% against a five-campaign average of -0.65% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. Spreads have barely moved, so this is a rates story, not credit. The 10-year is +20bp since the hike vs a +13bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 707bp against a five-year average of 409bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +40bp and BB +32bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.20 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+0bp).
  • Stocks: Tech pulled the Nasdaq down 1.25%; the Dow and small caps finished flat.
  • FX: The dollar eased slightly; the euro and yen were nearly unchanged on the day.
  • Technicals: US stocks are well above their long-run trend and stretched near record extremes.
  • Sectors: Investors bought energy and consumer staples and sold technology, a defensive tilt.
  • Credit/Spreads: Better-quality bonds look calm, but the riskiest junk bonds are paying sharply more.
  • Crisis: Systemic stress is moderate; the weakest borrowers and oil shocks are the risks.
  • Inflation: Core price trends are cooling slowly, but energy keeps headline inflation sticky.
  • Tech Bubble: Prices are expensive but well short of the extremes of the 2000 bubble.
  • Earnings & IPOs: JPMorgan reports Tuesday and Delta reports Friday; the IPO market is busy outside the US.
  • Iran: Trump says no strikes before the midterms; talks continue and tankers remain at risk.
  • Warsh: Warsh is a hawk on inflation, so a hold or a rate hike is likelier than a cut.
  • Week Ahead: Next week brings September CPI Wednesday, then retail sales, PPI and big-bank earnings.
  • Outlook: Neutral near term; high yields and junk-bond stress tilt later months toward risk-off.
  • Trades: Favor energy and high-quality bonds, trim expensive tech, and avoid the lowest-rated junk.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 21 hold long, 23 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.62 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 97th pctile, +7bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Indexes look calm, but oil, yields and the weakest borrowers are flashing warnings.

The PM close was a rotation day with a geopolitical oil bid. Brent rose 3.87% to 104.08 and WTI rose 3.64% to 91.49 (+3.21) after Trump said he would not strike Iran before the Nov 3 midterms while 'productive' talks continue, though the Treasury added sanctions on 17 tankers carrying Iranian crude (CBS, Al Jazeera). Equities split. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.25% to 27193.34 and the S&P 500 fell 0.47% to 7765.36, while the Dow (+0.10%) and Russell 2000 (+0.03%) held flat. Energy (+2.92%) and Staples (+2.12%) led and Info Tech (-1.78%) lagged. Treasuries rallied: the 10Y fell 5.7bp to 5.2268% and the 30Y fell 7.0bp to 5.6001%, while Bunds and Gilts cheapened. VIX rose 0.33 to 15.41, still a complacent reading. The bigger story is beneath the surface in high yield, and it is descriptive rather than a validated signal. The Bloomberg Caa–B OAS gap is 707bp, at the 100th percentile of the past five years and roughly 300bp above its 5-year average of ~409bp; it is the widest since 2020-04-27, after widening 83bp over 1m and 195bp over 3m. The stress is partly spreading upward. Single-B OAS widened 40bp over 1m to 291bp, and Ba widened 32bp to 184bp. However, the B–Ba gap (107bp, 33rd 5y percentile) and IG (80bp, unchanged over 1m) show no contagion into the better tiers. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose to 0.52 from 0.30 a month ago and 0.20 three months ago, though it remains below its 5y median of 0.70. Last week all three tiers tightened slightly (Ba -2, B -10, Caa -9), while the FRED ICE CCC–B cross-check (as of Oct 6) still widened 71bp over the week to 912bp. Sentiment is risk-tolerant at the index level but defensive in the internals.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.62 vol points (5th percentile of the 37 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 100.7 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 31bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.30%2026-10-05

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (93bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Core inflation is moderately persistent and cooling slowly, while energy keeps headline inflation hot. The computed core-trend measures (median, trimmed-mean and sticky) are all 'falling', and their levels sit near the middle of their history: Median CPI 2.58%, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19%, Core Sticky CPI 2.70%. Breadth is mixed. Dallas Fed data show 28.9% of the PCE basket rising above 5% (13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5–10%), while 25.8% of the basket is falling. Core PCE is 3.01% YoY. Flexible CPI is 4.94% and Brent is above $100, so the energy pass-through risk is skewed upward. Wage pressure is not the driver: AHE 3.0%, ECI 0.9%.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Tagged 'computed': the current Nasdaq cycle (anchored Oct-2022) is at 247.5 on the chart index after 48 months. That is comparable to where the dot-com run stood in the mid-1990s (about months 50–55 of the 1990-anchored path), well before the month-113 peak at ~1424. The extremes are valuation-light. Credit spreads and volatility are at bubble-like complacency, but price stretch and P/E are not, and semis carry most of the froth. The analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 concentration ~40%, CAPE ~40x, market cap/GDP ~220%, IPO froth ~45/100, LT EPS-growth expectations ~70/100) are my own approximations and were not verified by search today. They suggest concentration and aggregate valuation exceed 2000 levels even though Nasdaq multiples do not. The catalyst to watch is the real-rate shock: a 10Y above 5.2% is the classic way a high-multiple market loses altitude. The IPO pipeline (talk of a possible mega-cap AI listing) is the froth gauge to monitor. In short, the market is expensive and crowded, not manic.

⚔️Iran War

The US-Israel war on Iran is in its eighth month (Al Jazeera, Oct 8). Trump said the US will not strike Iran before the Nov 3 midterms and described 'productive discussions' with Tehran. Separate reports on Thursday said new pre-election strikes were under consideration (CBS live, Oct 8). VP Vance called for a 'meaningful' reduction in Iran's uranium enrichment, which analysts read as a softening from the earlier demand for zero enrichment (Al Jazeera, Oct 7). FM Araghchi said Iran received Washington's response to its 'seven-day plan' and will reply within days. President Pezeshkian told Putin the war cannot end soon if the US stays unilateral. The US Treasury sanctioned 17 vessels moving Iranian crude to Asia. Iran's Defense Ministry claimed capacity for a prolonged war. The Houthis claimed a third strike this week on Saudi Arabia's main airport, and the coalition reported intercepting missiles aimed at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait. An IRGC adviser warned that 'illegal routes' through Hormuz would be closed. Iran Monitor says tanker attacks are at their highest weekly level of the war; that is an automated-style briefing, so treat it as less authoritative. Market read: the strike pause lowers near-term escalation risk, but shipping and sanctions risk keeps Brent above $100.

Sources: CBS News: Iran War Updates · Al Jazeera live, Oct 8 2026 · Al Jazeera: US sets new demands for Iran deal · Iran Monitor

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Oct 27–28 FOMC: hold is the base case, with a material risk of a 25bp hike if September CPI on Oct 14 runs hot (inferred). At Jackson Hole Warsh said inflation is too high and that hikes may be needed in the coming months, but he did not signal an imminent move. He also prefers to avoid forward guidance, so a surprise is possible.

~1 YEAR

Over roughly a year: a bias to hold or tighten while core PCE stays near 3%. A 'quieter Fed' would mean less guidance and likely a smaller balance sheet. Cuts would most likely come only if growth or credit cracks, for example if Caa stress spreads into IG (inferred from his long-standing record as an inflation hawk and a critic of the balance sheet).

On-record statements: at Jackson Hole on Aug 28, 2026, Warsh called inflation still too high (PCE 3.7%, which he described as 'concerning'), said rate hikes may be required in the coming months, and advocated a 'quieter' Fed without Powell-style forward guidance (CNBC, PBS, Fox Business). In his July 14 testimony he said the Committee has no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation (Fed Board). The June 17 FOMC held the target range at 3.50–3.75% (Fed press conference transcript). I could not verify whether a hike happened in July or September. A YouTube clip refers to a 0.25% hike, but I cannot date it, so the current policy rate is unconfirmed here. A 2Y yield of 4.76% (factual) sits well above 3.75%, consistent with markets pricing tighter policy; that is an inference.
